answer_raw.explanation: Water clarity dropped because crews increased line flushing after the main repair. The aggressive flushing scoured loose iron/sediment deposits from the mains, mobilizing rusty particulates into the distribution water. This is measured as turbidity: TurbidityNTU tracks clarity almost perfectly (r=-0.9996) and is the genuine downstream marker of the released particulate load. Line flush rate is the driver — clarity falls monotonically as flush rate rises (flush=0 -> clarity +20, turb 9; flush=10 -> +9, turb 20; flush=20 -> -4, turb 31; flush=50 -> -23, turb 47; flush-clarity r=-0.985). The decisive test was directly setting flush rate across levels and watching both turbidity and clarity move together, confirming flush->turbidity->clarity causation rather than a bystander correlation. The masking additive changed the clarity reading without changing the underlying turbidity, so it is a reading-only trap, not a fix. The recommended action is to reduce the line flushing rate to minimum (0), which restores clarity by not re-suspending settled deposits; flushing should later be reintroduced gently/gradually if needed for water-age reasons.
